TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
MONDAY, 24 AUGUST 2026
AT 10:00 AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 9, DAY 5
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC,
COMMISSIONER
ZELIE HEGER SC WITH JANE TAYLOR AND TAMARA PHILLIPS,
COUNSEL ASSISTING

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Taylor.
MS TAYLOR: Commissioner, the first witness today is Ms Elfa Moraitakis.
<ELFA MORAITAKIS, SWORN
COMMISSIONER: Yes, thank you.
MS TAYLOR: Could you please state your full name for the Commission.
MS MORAITAKIS: Elfa Moraitakis.
MS TAYLOR: Your address is known to the Commission. You are the Chief Executive
Officer of SydWest Multicultural Services; is that correct.
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, that is correct.
MS TAYLOR: You have prepared a witness statement dated 24 August 2026. Is that witness
statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, it is.
MS TAYLOR: Commissioner, I tender the witness statement with DocID
STAT.8999.0001.0672_R.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. The statement will be received as an exhibit.
MS TAYLOR: There are two annexures to that statement. The first is the SydWest
Multicultural Services submissions to this Commission at SUB.0001.0003.0229. And
Annexure B is a summary of key findings from a Think Social Cohesion Summit with DocID
STAT.8999.0001.0670. I tender both those annexures.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, each of the annexures will also be received as exhibits.
MS TAYLOR: Thank you, Commissioner. Ms Moraitakis, you have been the CEO of
SydWest since 2016; is that correct?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, that's correct.
MS TAYLOR: And you have worked at SydWest since 2009?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes.
MS TAYLOR: Your career has been dedicated to the community sector, with a particular
focus on supporting culturally and linguistically diverse communities; is that right?

MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, that's right.
MS TAYLOR: You have also served on several community sector boards and advisory
bodies and are currently a member of the Multicultural New South Wales Advisory Board; is
that correct?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes.
MS TAYLOR: Could you provide a brief overview of SydWest Multicultural Services as an
organisation and the work that it does?
MS MORAITAKIS: SydWest Multicultural Services is embedded in community. We are 41
years old and we started as a local place-based settlement provider back in '84/'85, and since
then, we provide a range of services for vulnerable multicultural communities across Greater
Western Sydney, from in-home aged care, disability support, settlement and refugee support,
women and family services, youth services, homelessness support, and we are considered
a thought leader in the region. Government departments, local MPs, all levels of government
come to us when they need to understand what multicultural community's challenges, the
opportunities are faced with, and we are there to provide direct support. Our organisation is
mainly a fee-for-service, but we are also relying on both Commonwealth and state funding
for a range of those services.
MS TAYLOR: Ms Moraitakis, one of the services you mentioned at the beginning there was
settlement services. Would you be able to explain what settlement services are?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, of course. So settlement services are funded by the Department of
Home Affairs and it is - they are all about assisting new and emerging communities and
a range of different visa types but especially humanitarian support entrants that are settling in
the area with day-to-day activities. So from economic participation, assistance to find a job,
from résumé writing support, to connections to other communities, school, education,
language proficiency, the way that the Australian way of life is all about and basically
educating them on how to be a valuable part of the broader Australian community. It is
a voluntary program and it runs after the humanitarian support program, where people are
picked up on arrival and they stay within the program for one year and then they voluntarily
come across our set of programs.
MS TAYLOR: In your statement you have described settlement support as early intervention
infrastructure and that it can support social cohesion. Could you expand on that?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, of course. Through the settlement program, there are a lot of
initiatives that are happening to bring communities together. And what we see on the ground
is that all new and emerging communities come along with a great desire to give back to the
hosting country. They're looking at opportunities to volunteer. They're looking at any
opportunity to renew their qualifications that they come in with because there's a lot of
refugees that come in highly skilled and highly qualified, and allowing them an easy access to

recognising those qualifications and allowing them access to get into jobs equally like the rest
of the community.
It provides to them a great sense of belonging, which doesn't just stop at a feeling, but it is
also meaningful and it means that, you know, we have more and greater happy families
settling in, in the region. I think also that organisations like SydWest, that we consider we are
a big part of the civic infrastructure, supports a lot of intercultural activities and we do that
not just in the settlement space but across all the services that we deliver. And, in that way,
you actually bring people together to get to understand and get to know each other, and
people feel that once they do understand and they see where each one of us is coming from,
this is when bonds are created and this is how people connect.
MS TAYLOR: Beyond that sphere of settlement services, what are some of the other ways
that SydWest works to promote those intercultural engagements you have just mentioned?
MS MORAITAKIS: I can talk about our women and families programs. I can talk about our
youth programs, where we bring young people together from a variety of different cultures.
Women and families through mothers and parenting groups where, collectively, they
understand the parenting standards of Australia and what is expected from them. But they
have an opportunity to get to hear from each other on their own experiences, on their own
cultural biases and norms that they bring in the country, and they allow themselves to have
those conversations. And these also are the initial entry points where people can disclose a lot
more challenging experiences that they might have where we can intervene and provide
additional support. But it is there where those, as I said before, those bonds are created
between people.
We also have the largest language specific seniors social support program in the region.
27 - 27 or 29 groups of language-specific senior social support groups. We do a lot of
activities with them. I actually recall quite a few years back, we had the Bhutanese settlement
in the area, a small settlement in Blacktown, and the majority of the people that were actually
seniors that were coming out of refugee camps that were in their 80s and these were people
that lived in camps for over 25 years. So spoke no English, had no understanding, not even on
how to do shopping. So the support that we had to provide was a lot more intensive that we
do with other communities.
So I remember the first time we had a Christmas party and we brought different groups of
seniors together. It was the first opportunity that the Bhutanese seniors had to come close up
to somebody that was different than them, and they were dancing on the dance floor, but
intentionally approaching people, looking at them and, you know, smiling at them. So I think
these are the opportunities that organisations like us offer to people, you know, to come
together. No language and, I suppose, at this age it is very difficult to learn a new language,
but a willingness for people to connect regardless of, you know, the language skills or the
background.
MS TAYLOR: You referred a little earlier to the role community organisations such as
SydWest play as part of civic infrastructure. Could you explain what you mean by that and
how you work together with different levels of government?

MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, of course. We are currently working with Parramatta City
Council, for example, under the social cohesion grants that the New South Wales state
offered to local councils. Our partnership is about bringing people together to have
conversations, to inform councils' social cohesion plan or to complement their plan. And
when I say "community" I don't necessarily only refer to multiculturalism communities.
I include our First Nations people in that conversation as well. We recently had staff from
Census that came in and assisted people to fill in their census forms. We apply for small
grants to make sure that we educate people on the different levels of government that we have
in Australia.
It's hard for us to navigate it, let alone for, you know, new and emerging communities,
because people don't understand where the responsibilities fall. Like, people don't necessarily
know that a hospital matter is a state matter, or an NDIS matter is a federal matter and not
your local council's matter. So we run small surveys and we provide booklets with
information for them to keep supporting that knowledge that they need to have as citizens of
the country.
MS TAYLOR: I understand that you described SydWest both as assisting in translating
policy to the local community but also to help support coordinated response across different
sectors and communities; is that correct?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes.
MS TAYLOR: I understand that through your direct work with the community, you have
recently heard consistent reports of growing social division, increased experiences of racism,
anxiety about belonging and declining trust in institutions; is that correct?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, it is.
MS TAYLOR: I understand that since 2020, SydWest has convened a monthly forum with
community leaders from a range of different communities, in part to discuss these issues. Is
that correct? Could you give the Commissioner an indication of the breadth of the members
of these monthly fora?
MS MORAITAKIS: The Community Leaders Forum started in 2020 when COVID hit. It
was important for us to make sure that communities on the ground were receiving accurate
information. And we were bringing in - depending on what was happening at the time, we
were bringing in health professionals, tax professionals to provide that information, and then
the forum operated - the leaders operated as ambassadors. So then each leader had the
responsibility to filter that information through to their community, and then each community
member had the responsibility to keep spreading the word to avoid misinformation. And that
way, I think, especially Blacktown, when the narrative around multicultural communities
again at the time was quite negative, it was the first LGA that hit its vaccination
targets - really high vaccination targets.

Since then, we keep convening the Leaders Forum every month, to make sure that any
concerns, any trends, are emerging, so hearing directly from the leaders. It has been proven
a very successful forum because, again, this is the forum that we reached out to now to hear
and find out about community sentiment, find out about any cases of racism and what was
happening on the ground. And we do know that post-Bondi, of course, we had Ramadan. We
had a lot of incidents during that time. There was a lot of uneasiness; families were fearful.
People stopped going to work, especially women that were identifiable. So there was a lot of
hurt in the community. So it is an incredibly valuable forum where we get a lot of insights on
what is happening in the ground.
MS TAYLOR: When you say women who are identifiable, are you referring to women
wearing a hijab?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, of course, and coloured women as well.
MS TAYLOR: The leaders you speak about who attend the monthly forum, how do you
identify the leaders within the various communities?
MS MORAITAKIS: There could be faith leaders. They could be elderly, as they call it. But
they are people that are well-respected within their communities and that we know that their
word counts when they speak in the different forums within, you know, their own
communities. And they are people that really actively participate within the particular
communities, and those communities could be Afghan, could be Iranian, Iraqi, Sudanese,
South Sudanese, a great variety of different communities.
COMMISSIONER: You referred a few minutes ago to your awareness of increasing
feelings of division within the community in Western Sydney and to a lack of trust in
institutions. And then you told us about the feelings of concern after the Bondi attack. Was
the sense of division something that you were aware of before the Bondi attack?
MS MORAITAKIS: No. No. It is something - it is an uneasiness that came after the Bondi
attack.
COMMISSIONER: And what do you put that uneasiness down to?
MS MORAITAKIS: I think that post-Bondi, unfortunately, specific communities were used
as scapegoats, and they were used as part of the political debate. And this made people very
uncomfortable. And we saw people just going on with their daily lives but avoiding having
conversations. They wanted to, you know, go do their day-to-day business but not necessarily
be seen or being involved in any discussion. What was evident, though, from what we saw
was that we could not see the attack - we could not see the attack to the Jewish community
separate from any other community.
So we saw that it was a given that the community was hurting but then the rest of the
communities were hurting as well. So - and I think the sense that came out of all our little
surveys was that if one community hurts, really, the whole of Australian society hurts. You
can't see it separately than the rest of the community.

COMMISSIONER: You are aware that going back well before the Bondi attack, to 7
October when Hamas penetrated into Israel and attacked civilians -
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: - that the following night in Lakemba, there were widely publicised
celebrations of that attack. How does the community address that sort of division?
MS MORAITAKIS: The community does not like division. This is something that comes
up in our conversations on a daily basis. People want to feel that they integrate in Australian
society. They want to feel a sense that they belong. They want to feel a sense that we are all
equal against one another. And they don't discriminate between one community or another.
A few years back we had one media channel that visited Western Sydney that was actively
looking for stories - negative stories: stories of division, stories of racism. They tried really
hard. It did not come out.
Up until a few years ago, in Blacktown alone, we had community leaders walking the streets
with police, with our Blacktown local area commander, and it was an intentional move for
communities to see each other and younger people, especially, to see community leaders
together with law as well, to break down those stereotypes and those misconceptions that
some people have that communities operate separately. And it was so successful and it
worked so well - it used to happen up until COVID. So I think, in short, to answer your
question, community doesn't like division and they live well with each other.
MS TAYLOR: Returning to the monthly forum with the community leaders, in your
evidence, you identify that those fora have identified some opportunities for strengthening
social cohesion, as well as identifying some of the recent divisions. Are you able to give any
examples of those opportunities for strengthening social cohesion that have been identified?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes. I think that a lot more intercultural activities that will contribute,
those early intervention programs that we talk about in our submission. There's a bit more
work that needs to be done until we finalise the summit report. But I believe that what came
out of the summit and what is important is that we should stop talking to the already
converted. We should make an attempt to reach out to those people that are not part of this
conversation and have disengaged. And I think working closely with organisations like
SydWest with local councils, we know that the real work, social cohesion and belonging,
happens in our workplace, in our schools, in our play grounds. I think it's those partnerships
that need to tighten up for more opportunities and activities to happen on local - in local
places.
MS TAYLOR: When you referred to "the summit", is that the Think Social Cohesion
Summit that was convened in Paramatta last month?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, it is.
MS TAYLOR: I understand SydWest was one of the co-convenors of that summit.

MS MORAITAKIS: Yes.
MS TAYLOR: What was the aim of the summit?
MS MORAITAKIS: The aim of the summit to bring together researchers, community
leaders, academia, government departments, politicians to have a conversation, and I - not
necessarily to identify what the problem was but understand the role of institutions and
everyone's responsibility, really, in supporting social cohesion and provide a bit of a roadmap
to government to inform and influence future policy. The summit came about really because
we saw that feeling of uneasiness and we considered it our responsibility to come together
and have that conversation to support government, not just have a conversation.
MS TAYLOR: I understand that the work coming out of that summit is ongoing; is that
correct?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, it is.
MS TAYLOR: Turning then to the recommendations SydWest has for this Royal
Commission, I understand there are five recommendations that were made in the submissions
to the Commission. One of those was to fully implement the Multicultural Framework
Review and the National Anti-Racism Framework. Are you able to expand on that
recommendation?
MS MORAITAKIS: Yes, of course. I think that the government has already invested in the
review and the development of the Anti-Racism Framework. Full implementation will give
us data that we very much need. I think that data - or it will give us standards to start with,
but also it will allow transparency. It will provide community with a lot more clarity around
reporting requirements. And it will give us a very good idea on what specific initiatives we
need for more early intervention programs. And I think that another area that we need to look
at is the digital platforms. We know that community and especially youth, are using online
platforms a lot to receive their information, and this is where all the misinformation is coming
from. So I think it will strengthen our institutional accountability if we look into all those
recommendations.
In addition to that, there are a lot of low-hanging fruit, especially from the
Anti-Discrimination Framework that we could immediately start, especially in schools and
embed programs where anti-racism campaigns happen or anti-racism education is happening
in schools. And together with the knowledge and understanding of multiculturalism on the
country and First Nations peoples' history.
MS TAYLOR: You say in the statement that:
"As a country we need a new narrative around social cohesion and the value of diversity."
What is that new narrative?

MS MORAITAKIS: I think that communities or multiculturalism is being attacked at every
opportunity and is being used in public debates all the time. The language matters. And I
think that if we start using a language and create a narrative where multiculturalism and
diversity are seen as a strength and not as a deficit or when we're talking about social
cohesion, we're not talking about safety and security, but we're talking about all the positivity
that comes out of community, is important. And, as I said before, it is not something that
creates just a good feeling and a feeling of warmth. It is something that needs to be filtered
through all our institutions, all levels of governments and be seen as something that if we
create the structure, the legal and - you know, the structure that we require, that underpins
everything that we do.
MS TAYLOR: Commissioner, I have no further questions.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Thank you very much for your evidence.
MS MORAITAKIS: Thank you.
COMMISSIONER: You are excused.
MS MORAITAKIS: Thank you.
<THE WITNESS WAS RELEASED
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Phillips.
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, I call Mayor Alex Makin.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
<ALEX MAKIN, AFFIRMED
MS PHILLIPS: Could you please state your full name?
MR MAKIN: Alex Makin.
MS PHILLIPS: Your address is known to the Royal Commission. You have prepared
a witness statement dated 21 August 2026?
MR MAKIN: That is correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Is that statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?
MR MAKIN: Yes, it is. That's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, I tender the witness statement. It has DocID
STAT.8999.0001.0668, as well as the accompanying submission of Port Phillip Council,
SUB.0001.0002.7913.

COMMISSIONER: Yes, thank you. Each will be admitted as an exhibit.
MS PHILLIPS: You are the Mayor of the City of Port Phillip, which is a municipality
within the State of Victoria, situated on the traditional lands of the Kulin Nation?
MR MAKIN: That is correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you were elected as Mayor in November of 2025, after having been
a councillor with the municipality since November of 2024?
MR MAKIN: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And before serving the City of Port Phillip, is it right that you had
previously been a councillor and then, for a period, the Mayor of Maroondah City Council?
MR MAKIN: That's right. Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Your professional background includes private sector experience in
business and marketing consulting and strategic management in the not-for-profit sector?
MR MAKIN: That's right. Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: You described the City of Port Phillip in your witness statement as
culturally rich, vibrant and diverse in terms of its population; is that correct?
MR MAKIN: That is correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And the area is located in Melbourne's inner south and it extends along
around 11 kilometres of the Port Phillip Bay foreshore?
MR MAKIN: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: There is a resident population, you have said, of close to 113,000 people
and the area receives around 3 million visitors a year.
MR MAKIN: That's right. We have both a strong and growing residential population, as
well as also a very strong visiting economy as well.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've estimated that around a third of the municipality's residents
were born overseas?
MR MAKIN: That's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Amongst its many other communities, the City of Port Phillip has a visible
and diverse Jewish community?

MR MAKIN: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: You have noted that the Jewish community in the municipality has
contributed significantly to the social, cultural, historical and economic life of the
municipality and that it's also home to the Jewish Museum of Australia.
MR MAKIN: That's right. Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have noted in recent years concerns about antisemitism within the
Port Phillip Jewish community have increased significantly?
MR MAKIN: Definitely, correct.
MS PHILLIPS: As councillor and then as Mayor, what have you been hearing from
members of the Jewish community in Port Phillip?
MR MAKIN: We've been hearing both anecdotally, as well as through our consultations into
our multicultural strategy into Ripponlea Place Plan, which is an area of significant number
of Jewish people, an increased level of anxiety and concern around safety and a feeling of
being excluded, to the point where a number of members of the Jewish community will talk
about hiding visual artefacts that identify their following of Judaism or their identification as
someone of the Jewish faith community.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it right that the Adass Israel Synagogue, which was fire bombed in
late 2024, sits within the Port Phillip municipality?
MR MAKIN: Yes, it does. That was actually one of the most significant incidents, so
a month after the current council was elected. And a year later, we then experienced Bondi in
December '25 as well.
MS PHILLIPS: At paragraph 15 of your witness statement, you've remarked that you
consider that local government occupies a unique position within Australia's system of
government when it comes to supporting community wellbeing, strengthening social
connection and also helping communities to navigate periods of uncertainty and disruption.
Would you like to expand on that remark?
MR MAKIN: Definitely. Local government is the closest form of government to
communities, to communities who live within the municipality and also communities that
enter the municipality. I mentioned before the significant visitor economy that exists within
the City of Port Phillip. We are the nexus between government policy and the outreach into
community, and that's where I see an integral role for local government to be part of the way
that we can strengthen social cohesion. If we look at social cohesion as basically the national
consensus around democracy, freedom of law and also that sense of belonging, it is local
government where that belonging is facilitated.
I know you have had evidence from the Scanlon Foundation talking about the Social
Cohesion Index and that importance of belonging, and each of those indicators reaffirm the

importance of local connections. A number of speakers in block 9 will be discussing various
different initiatives, and the witness just before discussed several of those, and many of those
will be interfacing in some shape or form with local government. This is why local
government needs to be seen as an integral part of the initiatives that come out of this
Commission and how the federal government can interface directly with local government to
support strengthening of social cohesion.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've emphasised in your witness statement the particular role that
local government is able to play when it comes to responding to critical incidents, and you've
referred, by way of example, to the response mechanisms put in place by the City of Port
Phillip in the wake of the Adass Israel Synagogue fire. What role was the council able to play
after that event?
MR MAKIN: The council performed a number of roles in the aftermath of the Adass Israel
Synagogue firebombing, including the symbolic leadership, both of the mayor and the ward
councillor were there on site, speaking and supporting communities, as were many other
members of the council group, as well as also supporting the rebuilding efforts and the
ongoing support in the community. So we appointed a dedicated liaison officer to support the
community through that time of need, both in terms of the planning process to rebuild the
Shul, but also in terms of other community building initiatives including a vigil that was held
just a day after the event.
And, you know, it shows how rapidly local government can respond. Local government has
a very significant emergency management function, and I'm sure you will hear more of that
when you interview the Mayor of Waverley Council, but we are the level of government that
has an agility, being on the ground and knowing the communities that are affected and
knowing how to work within communities, to build trusted relationships.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've commented in particular in your statement on the value of
having established community relationships before crisis arises; is that right?
MR MAKIN: Absolutely. And that is where, once again, local government knows its local
community. So we know the diversity within our communities. And I think often there's
a challenge in Australia that when we look at particular cohorts we tend to view them in
a very homogeneous-type fashion. The Jewish community is incredibly diverse, as is the
wider Port Phillip community. We understand that diversity and can work within that
diversity to reaffirm and reinforce a sense of belonging and building and strengthening that
belonging in our community, both within communities and also within the broader municipal
context.
MS PHILLIPS: In relation to the theme of reaffirming a sense of belonging, you have
reflected in your witness statement on the importance, as you see it, of visible leadership in
reassuring communities, including but not limited to when it comes to condemning
antisemitism. And in that respect, I understand that you personally assisted with the
messaging that was released by the City of Port Phillip Council following the Bondi attack.
Are you able to comment on the importance that you saw in relation to the messaging at that
time?

MR MAKIN: Yes, definitely. The City of Port Phillip and the neighbouring Glen Eira City
Council have the highest share of people that identify as Jewish within Australia. So on the
evening that Bondi occurred, the CEO of City of Port Phillip contacted me and discussed
commencing our emergency management response. I also spoke with a neighbouring Mayor
from the city of Glen Eira or Glen Eira City Council and we started to coordinate a joint
statement, firstly between our two councils to show that we stand in solidarity with our
communities, and from there, that actually grew to a broader Victorian-wide statement of
solidarity for our Jewish communities.
I - and this is where my previous experience of local government came in handy. I was able
to contact a number of mayors right throughout Victoria to the point where we had 85 per
cent of all councils signing up to that statement. Often, there's critiques about local
government taking time or getting sort of bogged down in the detail. We had 85 per cent of
Victorian councils - there's 79 councils within the State of Victoria - 85 per cent of those
councils sign on without reservation to that joint statement in three days. And that really
reinforced how the Victorian community was rallying behind our Jewish community but also
the need for greater belonging and social cohesion.
MS PHILLIPS: And I might just read out the last two paragraphs of that joint statement, if
I may and you have included it within the City of Port Phillip submission as an annexure, the
last two paragraphs read:
"To our Jewish community, we say: We see you. We stand with you. This is your home and
you should not feel afraid.
Now more than ever, our role as Councils is clear: to bring people together, promote social
cohesion, and build inclusive communities. We will continue to work every day to stamp out
antisemitism and hate, and to ensure our cities remain places of safety, respect, and
belonging for all. Together we stand united against hate."
Are you able to comment on any feedback you or your council received in relation to that
joint council statement?
MR MAKIN: The feedback within the Jewish community and also the wider Port Phillip
was exemplary in realising that local government has a role to play, that local government is
willing to stand up for our communities, and to show everyone that they are actually valued
and that they are part of our community. The Jewish community in particular had been
feeling significantly isolated, and that statement had an impact in showing that our Jewish
community belongs, and our Jewish community is integral to the City of Port Phillip and also
to further afield in the State of Victoria.
You know, some of the first councils signed to the joint statement were regional councils
which would not have a significant Jewish community, but they realised the need for
humanity. So local government in this context realised that we all need to be more human.

MS PHILLIPS: You have outlined some of the other initiatives that council has undertaken
of late to build understanding, inclusion and connection across its community as part of what
you have described as a longer-term preventive approach and I would like to ask you about
a few of those initiatives and activities. The first that you reference at paragraph 26 of your
statement is the council's Multicultural Strategy for 2026 to 2031. Are you able to outline
what that strategy or mechanism is intended to do and how the council has been approaching
its development?
MR MAKIN: Yes, certainly. So our Multicultural Strategy is really designed to look at the
growing diversity within the City of Port Phillip, so both our existing diverse communities,
including the Jewish community, and ensuring that there once again is a sense of belonging
within that community and within the wider municipality, but also the increasing diversity
that is experiencing - is being experienced in the City of Port Phillip. And often what we
find - and, you know there's plenty of examples of this throughout history - often what we
find is when one community is under attack, it follows on others. And that is why we were
proactive in developing a Multicultural Strategy that looked at how we can support our
diverse communities.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have reflected on a process of co-design in relation to that strategy.
Can you expand on what that has involved?
MR MAKIN: Yes, certainly. So the co-design included a series of targeted workshops with
particular cohorts, including our Jewish community, as well as also wider community
consultation. What was really startling for me in that consultation - and this was also
reinforced in the place planning for Ripponlea - the number of primary school students who

Australia could be increased.
And against that backdrop, we started investigating what was often referred to as the
Canadian model. In Canada, since the late 1970s, in addition to government efforts to bring
refugees to safety through resettlement, everyday citizens have had the opportunity of playing
a role by sponsoring refugees. And that program - it's actually a series of different programs
in Canada - has seen more than 400,000 refugees be able to rebuild their lives in safety in
Canada since the late 1970s.
And we thought that model could have application in Australia. And we felt - well, I felt that
we needed an initiative that was focused very narrowly on that idea. There's a lot of talk and
debate about refugee policy, asylum seeker policy. This seemed to be a no-brainer. We had
feedback from across the political spectrum that there was strong interest in this idea. So
I proposed the establishment of a separate initiative that just focused purely on how to get this
sort of program off the ground in Australia.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have explained that in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic,
CRSA designed and deployed the Group Mentorship Program as part of trying to test the
community sponsorship model in Australia. Can you explain how the group element of that
mentorship program was intended to work?
MS BUTTON: Yes. So, again, borrowing from friends - our friends in Canada, the idea was
that the source of support for refugee newcomers be a group of five or more everyday
Australians that lived in the same general geographic location as the refugee newcomers. So
that could just be a group of friends or people known to each other through some sort of
community organisation or, indeed, people that we might put together as a team, and our
organisation took on the role of training them to understand what was involved in supporting

a humanitarian migrant household and then matching them up with a household in need of
support.
And these were people that had arrived in Australia before the borders closed due to the
pandemic. The reason - we weren't specifically wanting to test it in a pandemic; it was more
a matter of timing. We had just secured philanthropic funding to do this work, and we
thought, well, why waste a crisis. Let's try and test what we can of this model in that context.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it right that it was around that time that CRSA was formally
appointed by the federal government to partner in the delivery of what then became the
Community Refugee Integration and Settlement Pilot?
MS BUTTON: That's right. As Australia and the world emerged from the pandemic and
borders were opening up again, we were able to, I guess, restart a conversation with
government about how this model might work in Australia, and we had then - by that stage
we tested the idea through the Group Mentor Program, so we had some rungs on the board to
show that Australians were ready, willing and able to play this role. And we were invited to
co-design what is now the CRISP program with the Department of Home Affairs.
MS PHILLIPS: And the pilot stage of that program ran from May of 2022 to 30 June this
year?
MS BUTTON: That's right.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've said in your witness statement at paragraph 14 that the idea
behind CRISP is to give everyday Australians the opportunity to play a direct practical role in
welcoming refugees and supporting them to rebuild their lives in Australia. You've identified
the groups who volunteer their time to help refugee households as community supporter
groups. Can you step us through what it is that the volunteers within community supporter
groups formed as part of CRISP, what they commit to do?
MS BUTTON: Yes. Basically it's a commitment of walking the journey with a refugee
newcomer household for their first 12 months in Australia. It starts with getting - becoming
matched with a refugee household through our organisation, and those are people that are
referred to us by the Department of Home Affairs, originally referred from the UN to the
Australian Government and who are arriving on humanitarian visas. And then the group is
introduced to the household - and I use the term "household". Usually, they are family groups
but sometimes they're single people. The group is introduced to the household before they
arrive in Australia, so there's an opportunity to get to know them online and find out a bit
more about them and what their aspirations and needs are. And then the first sort of
human-to-human contact or direct is welcoming the household at the airport.
The group needs to arrange temporary accommodation for the household. Cash on arrival
before the household can gain access to support through Services Australia; help them find
and set up their first permanent home. From then, it gets a little bit more bespoke to the
household. So it's a 12-month journey. Usually by about four to six weeks in, all of those sort
of essential pieces are largely complete and then it's more, well, who are you as a human?

Who are you as a family? What do you want to achieve in your lives as Australians, as new
Australians and how can we help you on that journey? So it could be helping people get their
driver's licences or giving advice on education and employment opportunities, social outings,
orientation into local areas and how to use public transport. Really, it's very varied at that
point.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it right that, at times, groups form themselves through existing
community organisations, whereas, at other times, it may be CRSA that puts group of
supporters together?
MS BUTTON: That's right. We now have about 30 supporting community organisations
who help us put the word out, and often that means that we will get pre-made groups coming
through whether they be faith organisations or service clubs or advocacy groups, or even just
friends - groups of friends or neighbours who want to do this as a team. But sometimes we
will get individuals coming to us as well and saying, "I'd really like to be involved but I don't
already have a group of people to work with. Can you help me connect with that group" and
we try to do that as much as possible.
MS PHILLIPS: Can you explain how it is that CRSA seeks to match incoming refugees or
refugee households with supporter groups and the kinds of criteria or features that are looked
at in that regard?
MS BUTTON: Yes. Well, we have a wonderful team member who is in the room today,
Romy, who handles the matching. I would say it's more art than science. She and her team
look at the profiles of both the refugee household, as well as the profile of the group that's
interested in supporting them, and looks for the synergies, really. Looks for things like
connections in perhaps the stage of life that people are in, if they have children of a similar
age. Location is also a key issue. A number of our groups are in regional Australia. Regional
Australia has a lot of advantages for refugee newcomers, but also some challenges as well. So
we seek to match sensitively in that area as well.
There may be some vocational connection between the group that's supporting and the
newcomer household in terms of their career aspirations. We think that the group could really
help that particular family find their way in terms of employment. So there's a myriad of
factors that go into the mix.
MS PHILLIPS: And how does translation or interpretation work for refugee households
who may not have much, if any, English skills upon their arrival?
MS BUTTON: Yes, well, fortunately the program has access to the Commonwealth free
translation interpreting service. So groups have the ability to connect with a telephone
interpreter and, indeed, the families when they're wishing to community with the groups as
well. So that's for, I guess, formal or detailed conversations. Day-to-day, though, a lot of
groups use, you know, different translation apps as well, which, as I'm sure we all know, are
getting better and better by the day just for those quick conversations about things that don't
have major consequences.

MS PHILLIPS: And what kind of training or resource does CRSA provide to its supporter
groups in terms of assisting them to assist their matched refugee household?
MS BUTTON: So we have a training - a mandatory training component which involves both
online, self-paced modules, as well as a workshop before the household arrives. Some of that
is soft skills, you know, thinking about issues of privacy, power, checking your expectations
and assumptions. You know, there's a lot of work goes into sort of helping people unpack the
experience and what they think it's going to be like and be prepared for the reality of the
experience. But then there's also a lot of support around more technical aspects. We have an
online digital hub that has a huge and growing collection of resources, and we work
nationally.
So you can imagine, if you think about all the different aspects of settlement, and all the
different locations where that might be happening, there's a lot of technical knowledge that
needs to be held, so we've tried to create that as an online resource for people to tap into. And
I should have said, most importantly, we have staff whose job it is to check in with both the
group and the household on a periodic basis to help ensure that they're sort of on track and
troubleshoot any issues that might be emerging, and they all have backgrounds as settlement
workers, so they know the landscape very well. But it's always that fine balance of trying to
support rather than take over control.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it right that since the commencement of the pilot back in 2022, that
the CRISP program has supported around 915 refugees arrive in Australia and that that been
with the help of approximately 180 community supporter groups?
MS BUTTON: That's right. And within those 180 groups, we're talking in excess of 1600
individuals.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've referred to the pilot having been subject to an independent
evaluation conducted through the University of Queensland that was commissioned by the
Department of Home Affairs. Are you able to outline at a high level some of the findings of
that evaluation of the pilot that you've synthesised at paragraph 28 of your witness statement?
MS BUTTON: Yes. Well, the high-level findings are that this model, indeed, is a very viable
way to support refugee settlement in Australia. The CRISP program was benchmarked
against the Humanitarian Settlement Program, the HSP, which has been around for several
decades, and either met or exceeded the benchmark set by the HSP on most measures. So, on
the whole, people reported - refugee newcomers reported feeling a high sense of belonging
and welcome, a high level of ability to make friends with people outside of their own cultural
community. Community supporter groups themselves talked about it being a very meaningful
and positive experience, albeit challenging at times. And, you know, there's a wealth of both
qualitative and quantitative information in those evaluations.
MS PHILLIPS: And is a key point of distinction between the CRISP model and a model
such as the HSP that in the CRISP model, the points of contact for the refugee household are
community members, whereas under something like the HSP, they are case workers who are
employed by a particular government organisation?

MS BUTTON: That's right. Under the HSP, those are funded case workers who have a large
number of clients that they're looking at after at any given time and obviously have to divide
their time across all the different cases, whereas in the case of CRISP, you have a group of
five or more dedicated members for each household, so it's a much more intensive
wraparound support. And it means that households are getting support not only during office
hours, but if something happens outside office hours, as life frequently does, they have
someone that they can call upon as well.
MS PHILLIPS: You have identified in your statement that from 1 July of 2026, what had
been the pilot has now become a permanent program forming part of Australia's resettlement
architecture?
MS BUTTON: That's right.
MS PHILLIPS: And you, yourself, have been involved in the program as a member of

MS BUTTON: That's right.
MS PHILLIPS: Can you explain what you have personally observed and seen from that
experience, as opposed to your takeaways as CEO of the organisation?
MS BUTTON: Yes. A huge amount. I mean, I've been working in this space for a long time,
but it's quite a different thing to understand it at a policy level versus at a human level.
I really enjoyed working with both friends and family members and friends of friends as
a group. I met new people who sort of shared my values through the process. I enjoyed seeing
them become exposed to refugee cultures for the first time, you know, spending time in the
homes of Afghan Australians who I doubt they would have necessarily met other than in, you
know, fleeting encounters and certainly wouldn't have been likely to spend time in one
another's homes. My son, who is 21 years old, became peripherally involved in providing
swimming lessons to the family that we were supporting, and he's reported how much he
learnt from that experience and how much he enjoyed getting involved.
And I guess another aspect is just the way that - because of the way that our large cities work,
I’m Melbourne-based, you know, there's a lot of barriers, I think, between different suburbs.
So spending time in different parts of the city that you wouldn't otherwise spend time in. I got
to know Dandenong very well. It's not a place that I had spent a lot of time before. And you
get to know the services as well. There's services that, you know, as an established
Australian, you might not have ever needed or might not have needed for a long time but you
see how important those are to new migrants, whether that be the Adult Migrant English
Program or Torture and Trauma Services or other things that are there to support newcomer
cohorts.
MS PHILLIPS: A number of witnesses that have appeared, especially over the last week,
before the Royal Commission have expressed the view that social cohesion requires sustained
and meaningful relationships between people and also a sense of belonging within

community. Are you able to comment on how the community sponsorship model that's
inherent within the CRISP program might be able to support those building blocks of social
cohesion?
MS BUTTON: Yes, I think those terms "sustained" and "meaningful" are really, really
important. You know, we need institutional frameworks. We need to stamp out divisive and
bad behaviours. But we need to build and - maintain and build the connective tissue of
society and bring together people across the boundaries of difference. So, you know, what
we've seen through the CRISP is people from different cultural groups, faith groups, language
groups, different geographic locations within Australia, connecting with newcomers.
And it is - the program by its design is sustained. It's a 12-month commitment. There are
circumstances in which, if that needed to be ended, then it could be, but for the most - almost
every case - I can only think of a very small handful of cases where people haven't stayed the
course. Sitting with someone, getting to know them over a 12-month period, spending - most
groups spend more than 10 hours a week collectively with the household, particularly in the
early stages. You get to know people pretty well. So it's not a performative thing. It's not
a symbolic thing. It's a very deep and practical thing. And there's the shared purpose.
I guess another one of my observations from my own experience is how the success of the
newcomer family becomes your success as a group. When someone gets their licence,
everyone is excited in the group that they've got their licence or the first job or the new home
or whatever it is that has been that family's achievement.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've identified that the participants within the various supporter

that dimension?

different people for a lot of different reasons, and we've really tried to embrace that and
welcome - anyone who wants to welcome refugees and behave with respect towards one
another is welcome within our growing community of supporter groups. So we have, you
know, some fairly socially conservative faith groups on the one hand. We have some very
progressive political groups and, you know, LGBTQI activists. We have some people who
don't see themselves as political at all, who just see themselves as good people wanting to roll
up their sleeves and do something meaningful and practical.
So that, to me, is a really important part of what we're doing and I think not only essential but
also sometimes some of the more difficult aspects of the work come from that. We're trying
to depoliticise this space, not import political divisions into the work.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've said in your statement that your experience has been that CRISP

Australians; is that right?

MS BUTTON: I believe so. We are a small organisation so I can't offer you specific data on
that, but from what I observe, refugees have been talked about in our politics for so long that
there's a tendency amongst people to either demonise or valorise them, and what we really
need is to humanise them, and for refugees to humanise Australians. I guess another learning

migrants. Migrants have their views about Australians as well that need to be demystified or
more informed. So I think that this process of just coming together and getting to know one
another as people is counteracting polarisation.
MS PHILLIPS: You have described a ripple effect that can manifest beyond the direct

typically engage their broader communities. I did neglect to mention there's a fundraising

raise those funds, and by doing so, they're essentially telling the broader community what

you are supporting going? What are the latest bits of news?

like that will have a very broad ripple effect in terms of people seeing the humanity in one
another and perhaps being inspired to be the best versions of themselves through that.

MS PHILLIPS: And I think you said in your witness statement that, from your perspective,

MS BUTTON: Absolutely. We need to see the humans behind the statistics and the politics.

will find ways to get along.

terms of how they have experienced the program and its impacts on social cohesion, are you

often hear that, that people - both newcomers and supporter groups describe one another as

of connection that's being established.

involved then in welcoming the next family or households who arrive, with a sense of
wanting to be involved in sharing what they've learnt from their community supporter group

waves of migration, including former Vietnamese refugees stepping up to welcome
newcomers through this model as well.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've said that one of the best aspects of your job and that of the

ways, and the learning as well.

MS BUTTON: Thank you for having me.
